title: Using LLMs to Secure Source Code — Eugene Yan, Anthropic

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk presents a multi-agent harness with discovery, independent adversarial verification, triage, and patching agents structured as a feedback loop, which is fundamentally about agent architecture and harness design. The entire workflow is applied to security vulnerability finding, verification, triage, and patching in source code, matching the security and defense domain. The talk discusses production-scale scanning of 1000+ repos, operational bottlenecks around engineer attention, and practical deployment guidance to start this week. Prerequisites include threat modeling, Docker containerization, and SQL injection knowledge, indicating an intermediate-level audience. This is a conference presentation by Eugene Yan at the AI Engineer channel. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with specific character ranges and verbatim excerpts.

summary: Eugene Yan, a member of technical staff at Anthropic, presents a six-step workflow for LLM-assisted source code security, demonstrated on a five-line Python order-lookup endpoint with SQL injection. Three trends frame the talk: model capability shows a step-jump on cybersecurity benchmarks (UK AI Security Institute), vulnerability volumes surged dramatically (Mozilla Firefox rose from ~20 monthly fixes to 400 in April 2025, a 20x jump, with ~2/3 attributed to a frontier model), and the bottleneck shifted from finding bugs to verifying, triaging, and patching them. Anthropic's own scan of 1,000+ open source repos yielded 23,000 candidates, 6,200 high or critical, 1,600 reported to maintainers, and ~100 patched upstream. The six steps split into two setup steps and four loop steps. A written threat model alone raises true positive rates to ~90% because models have great code context but poor system context—design decisions and operational knowledge live only in engineers' heads. The sandbox provides isolation (VM, no egress, no cloud credentials) and reproducibility. Discovery optimizes for recall via context engineering, progressively simpler prompts, and giving the model tools to query APIs, read logs, and inspect source—approaching 100% true positive rate for one pentesting team. Verification optimizes for precision with an independent, adversarial agent that never sees discovery reasoning traces, assumes each vulnerability is false, and detonates the PoC in a fresh container. Triage protects the scarcest resource—engineer attention—through deduplication, severity calibration using magnitude and likelihood, and compensating controls from the threat model. Patching closes the loop with a validation ladder: original PoC stops working, test suite stays green, a fresh discovery agent re-attacks the patch, and a human confirms before merge. This generative verifier loop improves patch quality with each iteration, converting operational expense into capital expense. The entire pipeline resembles an ML pipeline: recall, precision, ranking, and closing the loop. Non-technical bottlenecks prove harder than technical ones: human attention doesn't scale, product and security engineers disagree on severity definitions, threat models remain tacit in people's heads, and fully automated patch review is still rare. Organizational mitigations include vulnerability routing to code owners, writing down severity rules collaboratively, and moving toward AI-generated patches with human verification. Yan's three takeaways: start this week on open source dependencies, learn interactively with hands on the wheel before automating, and remember that scanning was never the bottleneck—verification, triage, patching, and organizational processes are.

sections.title: Introduction and Three Trends
sections.summary: Eugene Yan introduces himself as Anthropic technical staff working with security teams and Claude. He outlines three trends: model capabilities, vulnerabilities found, and where the bottleneck is shifting.

sections.title: Cybersecurity Benchmarks and Mozilla's 20x Jump
sections.summary: Yan presents UK AI Security Institute cyber benchmarks showing a step-jump in model capability. Mozilla Firefox's monthly security fixes jumped from ~20 average to 400 in April 2025 (20x), with ~2/3 attributed to a frontier model. He references Log4Shell and Heartbleed for real-world stakes.

sections.title: Anthropic's Open Source Scan and Bottleneck Shift
sections.summary: Anthropic scanned 1,000+ open source repos: 23,000 candidates, 6,200 high/critical, 1,600 reported to maintainers, ~100 patched upstream. Finding vulnerabilities is now straightforward; the bottleneck shifted to verification, triage, and patching. Agentic harnesses changed the game.

sections.title: The Six Step Workflow Overview
sections.summary: Yan introduces the six-step workflow: two setup steps (threat model and sandbox) and four loop steps (discovery, verification, triage, patching). He introduces the running example: an order service where users type an ID to look up an order.

sections.title: Step 1: Threat Model and 90% True Positives
sections.summary: A documented threat model raises true positive rates to ~90%. Models have great code context but poor system context. Threat models can be bootstrapped by giving the model access to documents, code, past commits, and CVE patches, then asking it to interview the system expert.

sections.title: Step 2: Sandbox for Isolation and Reproducibility
sections.summary: The sandbox provides isolation (VM, no egress, no cloud credentials) and reproducibility (consistent baseline containers). Example sandbox: three Docker images (app, Postgres, Redis) with a security agent probing via HTTP from outside.

sections.title: Step 3: Discovery and the Five-Line SQL Injection
sections.summary: Discovery optimizes for recall via context engineering, simpler prompts (cut ~50% per model generation), and model tools (query API, read logs, read source)—one pentesting team approached 100% true positive rate. The running example: five-line Python order endpoint with SQL injection via string interpolation.

sections.title: Step 4: Independent Adversarial Verification
sections.summary: Verification optimizes for precision with an independent, adversarial agent that never sees discovery reasoning traces. It assumes each vulnerability is false and tries to confirm or disprove it. The verification agent detonates the PoC in a fresh container—given only line 4, it runs curl and sees exfiltrated customer PII, confirming the SQL injection.

sections.title: Step 5: Triage and Engineer Attention
sections.summary: Triage protects the scarcest resource: engineer attention. Sending all true vulnerabilities, including low severity, erodes trust. Triage includes deduplication (heuristics or model clustering), severity calibration (magnitude: ring zero vs ring one; likelihood: hoops for attacker), and compensating controls from the threat model. Example: agent rated high severity; human downgraded to low likelihood because an application firewall blocks SQL injections and the service is internal only—context not in code but in system design docs.

sections.title: Step 6: Patching and Closing the Loop
sections.summary: Patching closes the loop with a validation ladder: original PoC must stop working, existing test suite stays green, and a fresh discovery agent re-attacks the patch. This generative verifier loop—giving agents context and feedback—improves patch quality greatly. A human confirms before merge. The patch is a one-line fix moving the variable out of the Python string. Closing the loop converts operational expense into capital expense: the harness improves with each iteration by documenting compensating controls.

sections.title: ML Pipeline Analogy and Non-Technical Bottlenecks
sections.summary: The six steps mirror an ML pipeline: recall, precision, ranking, closing the loop. Non-technical problems are an order of magnitude harder. Scanning harness just needs more compute (solvable with money), but human attention doesn't scale. Organizational bottlenecks include: threat models stuck in people's heads needing interviews, product and security engineers disagreeing on severity definitions requiring collaborative rule-writing, and fully automated patch review still being rare.

sections.title: Organizational Bottlenecks and Three Takeaways
sections.summary: Three organizational bottlenecks: vulnerability routing (automate to code/service owners), severity calibration (write down rules collaboratively, give to agents), and patching bandwidth (move toward AI-generated patches with human verification). Three takeaways: start this week on open source dependencies, learn interactively with hands on the wheel (Claude Code or IDE) before automating, and don't just aim for scanning—verification, triage, patching, and organizational processes are the bottleneck. Resources include Claude Security, blog, and open source repos with interactive skills and autonomous harnesses.

demonstrations: Running example: order service with a five-line Python endpoint containing SQL injection via string interpolation on line 4, where user input flows directly into a SQL query
Threat model example for order service: key asset is customer PII data, entry point is the orders API, model suggests threat vectors including SQL injection and lack of authentication
Sandbox example for order service: three Docker images (app, Postgres database, Redis cache) with a security agent sitting outside the target boundary probing via HTTP
Verification example: verification agent given only line 4, runs curl command in fresh container, sees exfiltrated customer PII confirming SQL injection
Triage example: agent rates high severity (high impact, high likelihood); human downgrades to low likelihood because application firewall blocks SQL injections and service is internal only
Patching example: one-line fix moving variable out of Python string to reduce SQL injection surface, with compensating controls (firewall, internal-only) documented to close the loop
limitations: Building a representative sandbox of a system is quite difficult
Models have poor context of the system—design decisions and on-call knowledge are implicit and must be written down
High false positive rates previously made scaling impractical before agentic harnesses
Verification and triage remain the bottleneck, not scanning
Product engineers and security engineers may disagree on severity definitions, requiring collaborative rule-writing
Threat models are often stuck in people's heads and must be elicited through interviews
Fully automated patch review is still rare, especially for security issues
Sending product engineers all true vulnerabilities, including medium or low severity, can erode trust because they can't cope with the volume
